WMU 509 Aerial Ungulate  Survey Report (2016) 
Background 
The last survey conducted for WMU 509 was completed in December 2008 , using the random 
stratified block methodology  (prioritizing moose)  and produced a  moose population estimate of 
921 moose (±23.9%, 90% confidence interval) . During the 2008 survey, the stratification of blocks 
for moose corresponded to the stratification for white -tailed deer and thus enabled a robust 
population estimate for white -tailed deer. A total minimum count survey of elk in W MU 509 was 
conducted in February 2015. The population goal for moose in WMU 50 9 is 1,000, for white-tailed 
deer is 1,500 and for elk is 200 . The ‘Archery Only’ season  for most big game is from September  1 
to October 31 and the ‘General’ season is from Nove mber 1 to 30. Antlered and antlerless moose 
are managed on a limited entry hunt in both the ‘Archery Only’ and ‘General’ seasons in WMU 509. 
The 2015 hunting season  was the first year that moose hunting during the ‘Archery Only’  season 
required a special license. Prior to 2015 all cohorts of moose were available for unlimited ‘Archery 
Only’ season harvest with the general moose license. Mule deer (antlered and antlerless) are also 
managed through a limited entry ‘General’ season hunt. Hunting antlered mule deer in the ‘Archery 
Only’ season requires a special license  while antlerless mule deer may be hunted under a general 
license in the ‘Archery Only’  season.  White -tailed deer (antlered  and a ntlerless) are managed 
under ‘Archery Only’ and ‘General’ seasons, both only requiring a general license ; during the 2015 
hunting season, the  supplemental antlerless white-tailed deer license was valid for the harvest of 
one antlerless deer in WMU 509, reduced from 2 tags in 2014. Elk are available for harvest in WMU 
509 as well; 6+ point bulls may be harvested during the ‘Archery Only’ season with a general license 
but harvest of bull elk during the ‘General’ season requires the authority of a speci al license , 
similarly antlerless elk may be harvested during the ‘Archer y Only’ season under a general license 
but require a special license for the ‘General’ season.  
Survey Method 
The objective of this survey was to establish population estimates for mo ose and white-tailed deer 
and to obtain useful information on mule deer  and elk to guide management of these species .  
Note that observations of elk from this survey should not be used in comparison to the 2015 elk 
survey for WMU 509 to draw conclusions regarding the elk population in this unit  as survey 
methodology differs sig nificantly. Collection of age data and sex data was conducted where 
possible. Given this survey took place in early February  it is suspected that antler cast  was likely 
significant. As a result, antlerless adults were classified without sex information .  T ransects, 10 km 
in length (at times shorter when the lines ran into WMU boundaries) and oriented east -west, were 
established spatially throughout the WMU at 1.2 km intervals within a GIS environment.  Based on 
previous survey ungulate densities, transects were randomly selected until a minimum of 500 
kilometres of survey distance was achieved.  The survey was then flown using distance sampling 
methodology as described in the Distance Sampling Chapter of the Aerial Ungulate Survey Protocol 
Manual (ESRD, 2014).   
Results 
The survey was completed from February 1 to 3, 2016 and was concluded early to due to technical 
and weather constraints.  Total ungulates observed were  163 moose (77 groups on transect) , 157

white-tailed deer (46 groups on transect) , 2 mule deer and 97 elk (in 3 groups). Of the 150  moose 
that were successfully classified, 76 were cows, 50 were calves, 6 were antlered bulls (all small) and 
18 were non-antlered bulls.  Ninety -one antlerless white -tailed deer were classified as adult 
without sex identification, 9 had no classification ; 15 bucks were classified (4 small, 1 medium and 
10 large) along with 42 fawns. The 2 mule deer observed were a doe and her fawn.  In the 3 groups 
of elk observed, there were at total of 9 bulls (5 small and 4  medium), 2 cows, and a calf that were 
classified. Eighty-five antlerless elk were not classified due to safety constraints. Moose populations 
in WMU 509  appear stable since 2008, and higher than in the 1990s . White-tailed deer  surveys 
have not been conducted consistently in WMU 509, however, results of the 2008 survey suggests 
that white- tailed deer  populations have declined since. Mule deer continue to occur in low 
densities throughout the WMU in isolated pockets where preferr ed habitat exists. The only survey 
conducted in WMU 509 specific to elk was done so in February 2015 and yielded a total minimum 
count of 213 elk.   Population estimates and species densiti es for moose, white-tailed deer and elk 
are presented in Tables 1 – 3.
